# Gram-positive cocci

> *Staphylococci and streptococci cause illnesses as different as food poisoning and heart disease
> weeks after a sore throat. A few traits, and three ways of causing harm, account for nearly all of
> them.*

## One bacterium, three illnesses {#sec-gpc-hook}

Consider three people:

- A teenager scratches a mosquito bite. Two days later there is a **furuncle** (boil): a hot, swollen,
  pus-filled nodule.
- Forty wedding guests start vomiting two to three hours after lunch. Most are well by the next day.
- A young woman develops a high fever, a rash and **hypotension** (dangerously low blood pressure).

One organism, *Staphylococcus aureus*, can cause all three, by three different mechanisms. By the end
of this chapter you should be able to explain each of them from how the bacterium works.

## The group in one sentence {#sec-gpc-sentence}

Gram-positive cocci are thick-walled spheres that live on the skin and mucous membranes and cause harm
mainly when they get past a barrier. The table answers the book's six questions for the whole group;
the rest of the chapter shows how its members give different answers to the fifth.

| Question | Answer for the Gram-positive cocci |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | Thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane, so no LPS; many have a capsule or surface proteins that resist phagocytes |
| How does it get energy? | Staphylococci respire or ferment; streptococci and enterococci only ferment, but tolerate oxygen |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission; exchanges genes readily, which is how toxin genes and resistance spread |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Skin, nose, throat, mouth and gut of healthy people; spread by hands, droplets and contact |
| How does damage happen? | Three patterns: invasion with pus, toxins, and immune-mediated damage |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | A peptidoglycan wall, and the proteins that build it |

## Sorting the group {#sec-gpc-key}

A few traits separate every member of the group. The key below follows the order a laboratory uses,
but read each branch for what the trait means about the organism.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-key.yml"></div>

The three main organisms in the key each have a profile card below. The supporting organisms are
covered in one table at the end of the chapter.

## *Staphylococcus aureus*: three patterns of harm {#sec-gpc-aureus}

*S. aureus* lives in the nose of about one in three healthy people at any one time
[@kluytmans1997carriage]. It carries an unusually large set of virulence factors, including
coagulase, tissue-damaging enzymes and many toxins, and different factors produce different
illnesses.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Invasion with pus | Enters through a break in the skin; coagulase walls the bacteria in fibrin; neutrophils accumulate | Furuncle or abscess |
| Toxin without invasion | Multiplies in food left warm and releases a heat-stable toxin; the toxin, not the bacteria, causes the illness | Vomiting within hours of a meal [@argudin2010enterotoxins] |
| Toxin acting on the whole body | A **superantigen** activates a large fraction of the body's T cells at once | **Toxic shock syndrome**: fever, rash and hypotension [@llewelyn2002superantigens] |

These are the three people at the start of the chapter. The first has an infection. The second has no
infection at all, because the guests swallowed toxin already present in the food; this is an
**intoxication**. In the third, the host's own immune response does most of the damage.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-aureus.yml"></div>

A closely related staphylococcus lives on everyone's skin and causes harm in a quite different way.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-saureus-sepidermidis.yml"></div>

## *Streptococcus pyogenes*: tissue-damaging enzymes and delayed immune damage {#sec-gpc-pyogenes}

*S. pyogenes*, or group A streptococcus, lives on the throat and skin. Where *S. aureus* walls itself
in, *S. pyogenes* breaks tissue barriers down, and some of its most serious effects appear after the
infection has gone.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Spread through tissue | Enzymes digest clots, DNA and the ground substance between cells | **Cellulitis**: spreading infection of the skin and the tissue beneath it |
| Toxins | Streptolysins lyse cells; superantigens act as in *S. aureus* | Scarlet fever; streptococcal toxic shock syndrome |
| Immune-mediated damage, weeks later | Antibodies against the bacterium cross-react with the host's own tissue (**molecular mimicry**) | **Rheumatic fever**, which can scar the heart valves [@carapetis2016rheumatic] |

The third pattern is the clearest case in this book of the damage-response framework from
[*Microbes and their hosts*](../principles/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf): the bacteria are long gone,
and the host's immune response causes the damage.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-pyogenes.yml"></div>

## *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: the capsule {#sec-gpc-pneumoniae}

*S. pneumoniae* has fewer tissue-damaging weapons. It relies on its **capsule**, a slippery
polysaccharide coat that stops phagocytes engulfing it. Many healthy young children carry it in the
nasopharynx [@weiser2018pneumococcus]. Disease begins when it reaches an adjacent space, or the blood,
and multiplies there.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Multiplying where it does not belong | The capsule resists phagocytes; the host's inflammation fills the space | **Otitis media** (middle-ear infection), sinusitis, pneumonia |
| Invasion of the blood and meninges | The capsule protects the bacteria in the bloodstream, most effectively when host defences are weak | **Bacteraemia** (bacteria in the blood), meningitis |

The capsule also explains protection. Antibodies that coat the capsule allow phagocytes to engulf the
bacteria, so pneumococcal vaccines are made from capsular material. The capsule comes in about 100
types, so vaccines include the commonest ones.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

The two streptococci make a useful pair, because they illustrate two broad ways in which any pathogen
can cause harm.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-pyogenes-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

## Supporting organisms {#sec-gpc-supporting}

Each supporting organism can be understood as a variation on one of the main three. Learn the
separating trait and the reason it matters; the organ-system blocks will add the rest.

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Staphylococcus epidermidis* and other coagulase-negative staphylococci | Everyone's skin | No coagulase; few toxins; forms biofilm on plastic and metal | Infects devices such as catheters and prosthetic joints; contaminates blood cultures [@otto2009epidermidis] |
| *Streptococcus agalactiae* (group B) | Gut and vagina of about one in five pregnant women [@russell2017gbs] | Beta-haemolytic, Lancefield group B | Harmless to most adults; dangerous to **neonates** (newborn infants), who meet it at birth with immature defences |
| Viridans streptococci | Mouth | Alpha-haemolytic, no large capsule | Some ferment sugar to acid that causes **dental caries**; in the blood, they can adhere to damaged heart valves |
| *Enterococcus* | Gut | Tolerates bile and salt; intrinsically resistant to several drugs | Persists in hospitals; strains with acquired resistance are difficult to treat |

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "*S. aureus* is a hospital superbug"
Most *S. aureus* is neither resistant nor in hospitals: it lives harmlessly in the noses of about one
in three people. **MRSA** (meticillin-resistant *S. aureus*) is *S. aureus* that has acquired a gene
for an altered version of the protein targeted by a whole family of drugs, so the drugs bind it poorly
[@lakhundi2018mrsa]. Resistance is a trait that some strains carry, and it spread because drug use
selected the bacteria that already had it. [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../principles/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-resistance) explains the mechanism.
:::

## Later in the course {#sec-gpc-later}

You will meet these organisms again in the organ-system blocks. When you do, add each new fact to the
profile cards above.

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *S. aureus* | Skin and soft-tissue, bone and joint infections; **infective endocarditis** (infection of the heart valves); food safety; MRSA in pharmacology |
| *S. epidermidis* | Infections of devices and implants |
| *S. pyogenes* | Throat and skin infections; rheumatic heart disease in the cardiovascular block |
| *S. pneumoniae* | Otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia and meningitis; vaccines in immunology |
| *S. agalactiae* | Neonatal infection; screening in pregnancy |
| Viridans streptococci | Dental caries; infective endocarditis |
| *Enterococcus* | Urinary and healthcare-associated infections; resistance in pharmacology |
